argument_macro_structure.dominant_argument_form: Reductio ad absurdum via trilemma construction
argument_macro_structure.premise_explicitness: Mostly implicit; reconstructed from Hasker's commitments and the author's thought experiments

argumentative_quality.dialectical_reasonableness: High: engages with Hasker's own criteria, anticipates objections, and uses internal constraints rather than external assumptions
argumentative_quality.logical_relevance: All objections target the identity criterion and the coherence of emergent dualism across hiatuses
argumentative_quality.premise_acceptability: Premises are acceptable to Hasker or are defended by analogy and formal identity principles

distinctions_drawn: Reversible vs irreversible cessation of the field
Emergent dualism vs Cartesian substance dualism
Criterion of identity: field vs brain
explicit_definitions_given: Field of consciousness: emergent individual produced by brain configuration
Virtual existence: field's capacity to be regenerated by the same physical system after a hiatus

dialectical_engagement.objection_handling: Author anticipates objections (e.g., brain death, Corcoran's alternative, divine replacement) and shows each either fails or forces Hasker into a worse commitment
objections_raised: Hasker's virtual existence entails a contradiction with the necessity of identity
Hasker's resurrection and resuscitation accounts are incompatible when two fields can coexist
God's replacement of the field implies Cartesian-style 'added from outside' interaction and massive irregularities

method_and_evidence.evidence_type: A priori conceptual analysis, thought experiments, formal identity principle

philosophical_orientation.grounding: Analytic philosophy of mind and personal identity
philosophical_orientation.sentiment: Critical of Hasker's emergent dualism but not dismissive; aims to show internal inconsistency
philosophical_orientation.thematic_focus: Emergent dualism, personal identity, resurrection, unconsciousness, divine action

structural_organization.structure_type: Problem-solution-refutation: exposition, analogy, thought experiment, trilemma, conclusion

summary_of_core_decisions: The author's core decision is to test Hasker's field-of-consciousness criterion of personal identity against hiatuses in consciousness. By constructing a case where two fields of consciousness can exist (one preserved by God, one generated by the reanimated body), she forces a trilemma: either the brain is the criterion, or identity cannot survive hiatuses, or God must intervene in a way that contradicts Hasker's naturalism and anti-Cartesianism. Each option is unacceptable to Hasker, so emergent dualism is seriously flawed.

thesis_commitment.hedging_density_in_final_paragraph: Low; the conclusion is firm: 'this trilemma reveals a serious flaw'
